caption: Connectivity in Road Levels: A1140. A subtler connectivity issue in OSM affects coherent route creation. In Fig. 8, the footway isn't actually connected to the street, identifiable by checking node degrees. The red-circled node has degree 1, when degree 3 is expected at this three-line junction. This issue stems from improper tagging, common with pavement infrastructure where contributors may not understand junction implications.

caption_candidates.text: Connectivity in Road Levels: A1140. A subtler connectivity issue in OSM affects coherent route creation. In Fig. 8, the footway isn't actually connected to the street, identifiable by checking node degrees. The red-circled node has degree 1, when degree 3 is expected at this three-line junction. This issue stems from improper tagging, common with pavement infrastructure where contributors may not understand junction implications.

caption: Hidden Connectivity in OSM. These connectivity issues indicate OSM data requires cautious use and pre-processing. This can be achieved using GRASS or QGIS to snap nodes to the nearest line, ensuring footways connect to the road network. We developed a fix_rnet_connectivity function to address this issue, enhancing OSM data usability. The right side of Fig. 8 shows the corrected connection with proper node degrees. A.5. Road classification comparison between OS and OSM Princes Street demonstrates road classification differences between data sources. In OS data, Princes Street is an “A Road.” In OSM, it has three classifications: “tertiary,” “unclassified,” and “primary.” This inconsistency creates preprocessing challenges. Filtering an arterial network from OS data is straightforward using OS$road_function %in% c(“A Road”, “B Road”, “Minor Road”). With OSM, avoiding missed routes requires including more classifications: OSM$highway %in% c(“primary”, “primary_link”, “secondary”, “secondary_link”, “tertiary”, “tertiary_link”, “unclassified”). As Fig. 9 shows, the filtered OS network is concise, while the OSM network contains scattered, disconnected lines. Some streets are missing in OSM, like Inverleith Place (classified as “residential”). Such misclassifications can cause popular cycling routes to be overlooked. The abundance of un­ classified OSM roads further complicates network interpretation.

caption: Road Classification of Princes Street. A.6. Off-Road Path Coverage Comparison between OS and OSM Fig. 10 highlights another major difference: off-road path coverage. OS data doesn't consistently include cycling infrastructure like park connectors or off-street trails, while OSM often maps these in detail. These routes are vital for complete cycling networks, particularly in urban areas where segregated cycleways and park trails provide pleasant, direct connections.
